chapters.heading: UNITED STATES CAPITOL POLICE REFORM AND ACCOUNTABILITY

sections.heading: Removals, detentions, and arrests
paragraphs: (a) The Capitol Police may remove a person from the United States Capitol Buildings and Grounds, a House-controlled area, a Senate-controlled area, a shared congressional area, or any area under temporary jurisdiction where the person is unlawfully present, refuses to comply with lawful access rules, disrupts congressional business, obstructs an entrance or proceeding, threatens the safety of another person, damages property, interferes with a lawful security measure, or refuses a lawful order to leave.

(b) A person may be directed to leave by an officer of the Capitol Police, the Chief, the Board, the relevant Sergeant at Arms, the Speaker, the President pro tempore, a Presiding Officer, or any other officer acting under lawful authority.

(c) Where practicable, a person shall be warned and given a reasonable opportunity to comply before being removed. A warning shall not be required where immediate action is necessary to protect life, prevent injury, stop violence, prevent intimidation, secure a proceeding, prevent destruction of property, stop active obstruction, or respond to an emergency.

(d) The Capitol Police may use reasonable and proportionate force to remove a person who refuses to comply with a lawful order to leave. The force used shall be limited to what is necessary to carry out the removal, protect persons or property, preserve order, or prevent further obstruction.

(e) Removal from a space shall not, by itself, constitute an arrest. A person removed under this section may be released outside the affected area unless further detention or arrest is authorized by law.

(f) The Capitol Police may temporarily detain a person where detention is reasonably necessary to prevent immediate harm, stop active obstruction, investigate a suspected violation of law, identify a person involved in a security incident, execute a lawful order, prevent escape from a lawful stop, or hold the person pending transfer to another lawful authority.

(g) A temporary detention shall be limited in duration, scope, and manner to the reason for the detention. A person detained under this section shall not be held longer than reasonably necessary to address the threat, complete the investigation, transfer custody, or resolve the security incident.

(h) The Capitol Police may arrest a person for any violation of federal law committed within the jurisdiction of the Capitol Police, any offense committed in the presence of an officer where arrest is authorized by law, or any other offense for which the Capitol Police has lawful arrest authority.

(i) The Capitol Police may arrest a person outside the United States Capitol Buildings and Grounds only where the arrest is connected to temporary jurisdiction, protective services, an official congressional function, a threat against Congress or a protected person, fresh pursuit from within Capitol Police jurisdiction, assistance to another law enforcement agency, or another lawful basis recognized under this Act.

(j) The Capitol Police may transfer a person arrested or detained under this section to the custody of another federal, State, or local law enforcement agency where such transfer is lawful and appropriate.

(k) A Member of Congress shall not be arrested, detained, removed from the floor of that Member’s House, prevented from voting, prevented from speaking when recognized, prevented from entering the chamber of that Member’s House, or otherwise interfered with by the Capitol Police for conduct arising solely from debate, voting, speech, a legislative act, participation in a congressional proceeding, exercise of a right or privilege under the Constitution, or exercise of a right or privilege under the rules of either House.

(l) The preceding subsection shall not be construed to protect assault, battery, threats of violence, possession or use of a weapon in violation of law or lawful rule, bribery, extortion, destruction of property, obstruction unrelated to a protected legislative act, active violence, attempted violence, intimidation of a witness, unlawful entry into a restricted area, or any other non-legislative criminal conduct. (m)A Member of Congress may be removed, detained, or arrested where immediate action is necessary to prevent death, serious bodily injury, active violence, attempted violence, an imminent threat to another person, an imminent threat to a congressional proceeding, or another emergency that cannot reasonably be addressed through ordinary chamber procedure.

(n) Where practicable, and where doing so would not endanger life, permit violence, allow escape, impair emergency response, or prevent the securing of a threat, the Capitol Police shall coordinate with the relevant Sergeant at Arms or Presiding Officer before removing, detaining, or arresting a Member of Congress in connection with conduct occurring in or near a chamber, committee room, hearing room, gallery, cloakroom, or other space directly connected to a congressional proceeding.

(o) Nothing in this section shall be construed to authorize the Capitol Police to interfere with debate, voting, recognition, parliamentary procedure, legislative acts, or the lawful privileges of either House, except where immediate action is necessary under this Act to prevent death, serious bodily injury, active violence, attempted violence, or an imminent threat.

(p) Any removal, detention, or arrest of a Member of Congress shall be reported as soon as practicable to the Speaker, the President pro tempore, the relevant Sergeant at Arms, the Chief, and the Board.
(q) Any arrest or detention of a Member of Congress shall be reported as soon as practicable to the Speaker, the President pro tempore, the relevant Sergeant at Arms, the Chief, and the Board.

(r) Where a removal, detention, or arrest occurs during a congressional proceeding, committee proceeding, joint session, hearing, or other official function, the Chief shall ensure that the relevant Sergeant at Arms is notified as soon as practicable.

(s) The Chief shall maintain records of removals, detentions, and arrests carried out under this section. Such records shall include the date, location, reason for action, authority relied upon, officers involved, whether force was used, whether injury occurred, whether property was damaged, whether the person was released or transferred, and whether the incident affected a congressional proceeding.
(t) Records concerning removals, detentions, and arrests may be reviewed by the Board and by any committee or officer authorized by either House.

sections.heading: Use of force
paragraphs: (a) An officer of the Capitol Police may use only the force that is reasonable, necessary, and proportionate under the circumstances to protect life, prevent injury, stop an active threat, make a lawful arrest, carry out a lawful detention, remove a person lawfully ordered to leave, prevent escape from lawful custody, protect property, or restore order during a disruption of congressional business.

(b) Force shall be limited to the level reasonably necessary to accomplish the lawful objective. An officer shall use de-escalation, verbal direction, warnings, distance, cover, containment, or other reasonable alternatives where practicable before using force.
(c) Deadly force may be used only where the officer reasonably believes that such force is necessary to prevent death or serious bodily injury to the officer or another person.
(d) Force shall not be used as punishment, retaliation, intimidation, political pressure, discipline, or to compel agreement with any political, legislative, or personal position.

(e) The Chief shall issue regulations governing use of force, de-escalation, reporting, review, officer discipline, equipment, less-lethal tools, firearms, restraints, crowd control, removals, arrests, detentions, and emergency response.

(f) Use-of-force regulations shall include standards for warnings, proportionality, supervisor notification, preservation of evidence, review of body-worn or security footage where available, and referral for discipline or investigation where misconduct may have occurred.

(g) An officer who uses force resulting in injury, death, detention, arrest, removal from a congressional proceeding, discharge of a firearm, use of a less-lethal weapon, or formal complaint shall complete an incident report as soon as practicable.

(h) The incident report shall identify the date, time, location, reason for the use of force, type of force used, persons involved, officers involved, witnesses known to the officer, injuries known to the officer, whether any arrest or detention occurred, and whether the incident affected a congressional proceeding.

(i) Where force results in serious bodily injury, death, discharge of a firearm, use of force against a Member of Congress, or force during a chamber proceeding, joint session, hearing, or committee proceeding, the Chief shall notify the Board and the relevant Sergeant at Arms as soon as practicable.

(j) The Chief shall ensure that uses of force are reviewed by supervisors and that serious uses of force are reviewed through a formal process sufficient to determine whether the force complied with law, this Act, regulations, training, and the lawful duties of the Capitol Police.

(k) The Board may review any use of force involving death, serious injury, a Member of Congress, a congressional officer, a witness, a chamber proceeding, a joint session, a major security incident, or a complaint alleging excessive force.

(l) The Chief shall ensure that all officers receive regular training on use of force, de-escalation, lawful removals, lawful arrests, lawful detentions, protection of congressional proceedings, member privileges, emergency response, and political neutrality.
